query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing minor-element doping at the internal boundaries of a eutectic high-entropy alloy can enhance boundary cohesion, alleviating local stress concentrations and microcracking to improve room-temperature ductility while preserving or slightly increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibits limited ductility and brittleness under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Co-deposition or infiltration doping with minor elements (e.g., at 1000–1100°C in an inert atmosphere) to modify and strengthen internal boundaries.
generation.conditions: Perform doping at elevated temperature for sufficient time to achieve uniform distribution of minor alloying additions, then cool and conduct room-temperature tensile tests under standard strain rate conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined chemistries at phase boundaries that reduce dislocation pile-ups and mitigate stress concentrations, enabling smoother dislocation transfer across interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Minor-element dopants increase boundary cohesive energy and reduce microcrack initiation at interphase boundaries, improving load sharing and lowering the probability of brittle failure during tensile deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced tensile ductility, quantifiably exceeding that of the baseline alloy (e.g., >10% increase in elongation), with maintained or slightly increased yield strength relative to the untreated material.
generation.baseline: Undoped eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical lamella, showing premature microcracking and brittle fracture under tension.
generation.boundary: Beneficial doping effects persist at room temperature and moderate strain rates; the impact of higher test temperatures or complex loading paths remains to be further validated.
generation.uncertainty: Exact choice and concentration of dopants must be optimized for maximum benefit; outcomes can vary based on diffusion kinetics and microstructural evolutions.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two batches of the same eutectic HEA: one doped at 1000–1100°C with minor elements to strengthen grain and phase boundaries, and one undoped as a control. Perform standard tensile tests at room temperature on both sets of specimens.
measurements: Tensile strength and elongation to fracture
Fracture surface characterization (SEM, TEM) to observe threshold for microcrack formation
Comparative analysis of boundary elemental composition using EDS or atom probe tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy does not exhibit higher boundary cohesion (e.g., fewer microcracks, higher measured boundary strength) or fails to demonstrate equal or improved strength and ductility compared to the undoped control, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.
